A woman offers herself to the Prophet, and he marries her to a man who asks, for what he knows of the Quran by heart.
Aisha says verse 4.128 concerns a man who dislikes his wife and means to divorce her, and she gives up her rights so that he keeps her.
When Ma'qil bin Yasar refused to let his divorced sister remarry her former husband after her waiting period, the verse forbidding such prevention was revealed.
Aisha said the verse on a wife fearing cruelty or desertion concerns a husband who wants to divorce her, while she tells him she frees him as regards herself.
A woman offers herself to the Prophet, who marries her to a man owning not even an iron ring for the amount of the Quran he knows by heart.
Three men resolve on endless prayer, fasting and celibacy, but the Prophet says he sleeps and marries; Aisha explains the orphan-girl verse; young people who can marry should.
Wifeless men on campaigns are forbidden castration and Uthman bin Maz'un celibacy, temporary marriage is then allowed, Abdur-Rahman marries in Medina, and Abu Huraira is told the pen has dried.
Aisha hints she was the Prophet's only virgin bride, shown to him in dreams; he asks Abu Bakr for her, asks Jabir why not a virgin, and praises Quraysh women.
A man who educates, frees and marries his slave girl gets double reward; a tyrant gave Sara Hajar; the Prophet freed Safiyya and made her freedom her bridal gift.
A man with nothing is married for the Quran he knows, Abu Hudhaifa weds his niece to the freed slave Salim, and a woman should be married for her religion.
Ibn Abbas lists women unlawful by blood and marriage; none may wed two sisters or a woman and her aunt together, nor swap daughters in marriage without bridal gift.
Ali reports the Prophet forbade temporary marriage at Khaibar; Ibn Abbas allowed it in need, it was allowed in an army for three nights, and Ali said it was cancelled.
Women offer themselves to the Prophet in marriage, one praised by Anas; Umar offers Hafsa to Uthman and Abu Bakr; Durra is unlawful to the Prophet as a foster niece.
One may hint, not openly declare, a proposal to a widow in her waiting period; the Prophet saw Aisha in a dream and looked closely at a woman offering herself.
Aisha says the Prophet ended pre-Islamic marriages except asking a guardian for a woman's hand; guardians may not stop orphan girls or a divorced sister marrying, and Umar offers Hafsa.
A matron must be consulted, a virgin's silence is consent; Khansa's marriage against her wish is annulled; the Prophet marries a woman to a man for the Quran he knows.
No man should propose to a woman engaged to his brother or undercut another's bargain, and suspicion and spying are forbidden; Abu Bakr kept secret the Prophet's mention of Hafsa.
After Ar-Rubayyi's wedding the Prophet sits with her while girls beat tambourines mourning her father, killed at Badr, and he stops a line claiming he knows tomorrow.
A prophet bars grooms yet to consummate from his campaign; the Prophet consummates with Aisha and Safiyya, tells Jabir he will have Anmat, and notes the Ansar like wedding amusement.
Ibn Umar held marrying a woman who calls Jesus her Lord unlawful; an emigrant woman from warring pagans could marry after one menses; Umar and Iyad divorced wives who remarried.
Jabir, whose father left seven or nine daughters, married a matron rather than a virgin so she could look after them, and the Prophet blessed him.
The Prophet invoked blessing on the marriages of Abdur-Rahman bin Auf and Jabir, and taught a husband words seeking protection from Satan before intercourse, protecting any child conceived.
The Prophet annulled the marriage of Khansa, given by her father against her wish, and said a woman's consent is required, a shy virgin's silence counting as consent.
The Prophet forbade Shighar, exchanging daughters or sisters in marriage without Mahr, and Mut'a marriage at Khaibar, while some people judged such marriages made by trick valid or invalid.
A virgin or matron is married only with her consent, a virgin's silence counting, and Khansa's forced marriage was cancelled, though some people upheld marriages faked through false witnesses.
